write_incoming_message.text:
'Across the known systems, shipyard operators are reporting a sharp increase in unauthorized salvage work around repair berths, construction queues, and abandoned holding yards.

The incidents appear to follow a similar pattern. Small EVA crews approach disabled or ownerless ships, use compact cutting beams to free valuable components, and depart before yard security can establish ownership, liability, or even a repair ticket. In several reported cases, technicians claim the same crews later returned with bonding rigs to refit recovered parts onto privately owned vessels.

Mora Tilen, a spokesperson for an independent shipyard consortium, spoke to GalNet about the growing concern.

"This is not salvage in any responsible sense. It is unlicensed shipbuilding in a pressure suit. These crews are bypassing certification, warranty records, safety checks, and every fee that keeps a yard operational. The fact that some of them appear unusually well supplied only makes the matter more troubling."

Port authorities have stopped short of naming a single supplier, but several investigations now point to anonymous dockside dealers moving compact industrial tools and volatile field catalysts through black-market channels. Yard officials insist this trade is limited and dangerous. Independent captains, predictably, are less convinced.

GalNet can only note that the argument is unlikely to fade while damaged hulls continue to outnumber available repair crews. For pilots willing to trust a dealer over a dockmaster, the warning may read less like a prohibition and more like a shopping list.

Ralen Voss
Industrial Affairs Correspondent, GalNet'
